Home by Bedtime

It has no engine, no windows, and a horn that has never once worked. It is also, by the only honest measure that exists, the best-selling car in America. A love letter to the Little Tikes Cozy Coupe — and to the man who drew it.

By Grayson Kollen  ·  Fun Facts  ·  11 min read

There is a vehicle I can say, with something close to 95 percent certainty, is sitting in a driveway near you right now. Behind a picket fence, behind a closed gate, on a patch of suburban lawn from Ohio to Oxfordshire — it is there. No, it is not a Camry. It is not an Accord. It is not, God help us, a Prius. It is a two-door coupe, and it has brought more joy to more human beings than any other vehicle on planet Earth.

I will contest that claim against anyone. There is only one caveat: you have to be under the age of seven, or a parent. Everyone else, please take a number.

It's the Cozy Coupe. The red two-door with the open-air feel — and by open-air I mean no windows at all, ever, a design department that looked at glass and said no thank you. It has a sturdy, stylish yellow roof. It has a horn that never works. It has front wheels that are entirely independent of one another and, crucially, not attached to the steering wheel — a genuine styling crime that turns out to be a safety feature, because the car does not go fast and was quite deliberately built not to.

"It kind of breaks all the rules for car styling," its designer once said. He meant it as a confession. It reads now like a manifesto.

01The best-selling car in America. This is not a joke.

Let's get the astonishing part out of the way, because most people assume it's a gag and it is not. In 2008, the Little Tikes Company sold 457,000 Cozy Coupes — and in doing so outsold the Toyota Camry and the Honda Accord, the two best-selling actual automobiles in the United States. It edged the Camry by roughly twenty thousand cars. A foot-powered plastic toddler wagon beat the family sedan that America builds its entire idea of "sensible" around.

And 2008 wasn't a fluke. Back in 1991 the Coupe moved around 500,000 units, comfortably ahead of the 399,000 Accords and 299,000 Ford Tauruses sold that year. The New York Times flatly called it the world's best-selling car for much of the 1990s. By 1997 it was shifting 313,000 in the States and another 100,000 in Britain — which, if you were reckless enough to rank it against the real ones, would have made it the fifth-best-selling car in the country.

Little Tikes knew exactly what it had. In a 1993 magazine ad — a real one, which I am staring at as I write this — they parked a Cozy Coupe on a mesa in Monument Valley at golden hour, the kind of cathedral-of-the-West cinematography Ford spends millions on, and ran a single line beneath it:

"The best-selling car in America has to be home by bedtime."

Run the numbers all the way out and they get sillier. By its thirtieth birthday in 2009, more than ten million had rolled out into the world. A toy-industry trade figure put the global total at 22 million by 2012. That is Volkswagen Beetle territory. Writers with a sense of humor have noted that on a pure cumulative basis the little red coupe has out-produced the Ford Model T — and you should take that with the wink it's offered with, but you should also notice nobody's been able to definitively wave it away.

03The man who drew it never rode in a car as a kid

Here is where the joke stops and the story gets genuinely good. The Cozy Coupe was designed by a man named Jim Mariol, and he did not come to it lightly.

Mariol was born in Canton, Ohio, in 1930 — a Depression baby. His father, trying to keep the family afloat, had to sell the family car before Jim was even born, so as a small boy he rarely rode in one at all. He just watched them go by his house, dreaming, the way certain kids do. He decided he would design cars someday.

And he almost did the ordinary version of that dream. A car he sketched as a teenager won him a scholarship in 1947. He studied industrial design at the University of Cincinnati and co-oped at Chrysler, where a young Jim Mariol drew hubcaps, steering wheels, and hood ornaments for real Detroit iron — before the Army pulled him out mid-degree to serve in Korea. He came back, tended bar for a while, and eventually founded a design firm called Design Alliance, cranking out shop vacs and radios and campers for Procter & Gamble and Emerson Electric. Good, unglamorous, invisible work.

Then one day in 1979, sitting in his office, he pushed himself backward across the floor in his rolling desk chair — feet down, scooting, the way every restless adult has done since the swivel chair was invented — and had the idea. What if a kid could do this? What if the car was the child, and the child was the engine?

He spent his whole life wanting to design a car. He finally did — and it turned out to be the most successful one anybody has ever built.

He took it to Little Tikes founder Tom Murdough, whose entire design philosophy was two words: keep it simple. Mariol built the full-size prototype himself, in-house, and did the engineering for the plastic molds too. He had his own grandchildren test it. The first model was red with a black roof — and here's the detail I love most: he added the stubby back end and those bigger rear wheels not only to give it a little "trunk," but to keep the whole thing from tipping over when a toddler leaned. So yes — when you look at those two independent, purposeless-looking front wheels and think surely that's a safety thing, you're right. The whole rear half of the car is quiet, deliberate, load-bearing engineering, disguised as a cartoon. He patented it in 1982 as, officially, a "Toy Automobile."

Within four years of the Coupe's launch, Little Tikes' total sales climbed from $15 million to nearly $43 million. In one year in the late 1980s, Mariol personally made more than a million dollars in royalties. The kid who never got to ride in a car built the one that ended up in more driveways than any car in history.

Then it did it again in 2008 — 457,000 Coupes to the Camry's roughly 437,000. The same little car, a full generation later, still winning. There is no other product in the American economy that has quietly humiliated Toyota twice, seventeen years apart, using nothing but molded plastic and the legs of two-year-olds.

05The joy. This is the actual point.

Now, back to the joy — because that's the real reason the numbers look the way they do. Every child who has ever sat in a Cozy Coupe has produced the single greatest smile in that child's entire catalog of smiles. Not a big smile. The smile. The one you'd trade a great deal to see again.

And here's the thing I keep coming back to, the thing that makes this piece matter more than a listicle. No matter what car you drive, what motorcycle you ride, what adventure or activity you have lined up for your grown-up weekend — it cannot beat a child's raw joy for life, or their joy in the exact thing they are doing at that moment. It just can't. It's not close. A kid in a $19 plastic car, feet slapping the pavement, going nowhere at two miles an hour, is having a better time than you will have in anything with a badge on the hood. That's not a knock on the good stuff. It's just the truth, and the Cozy Coupe is where you see it most clearly.

06The menace. (Every love letter has a but.)

For the parent, the joy has one strict condition, and the condition is a single preposition: your child must be in the car. In. Watching your kid in the Cozy Coupe is bliss.

Outside of that arrangement, this vehicle is a menace. It is always in the way. It is awkward to pick up. It hits your shin — every time, without fail, even when you have taken specific, deliberate precautions for it not to. You will move it three feet to the left precisely so it can find a new angle from which to hit your shin.

And the moment the child climbs out, the car somehow grows in size. Fully occupied it is a delight; empty it will not fit anywhere, cannot be stored, cannot be moved in any graceful way. It gets wedged in doorways. It gets stuck under furniture that it plainly cleared on the way in. Leave it outside for one night and it collects more standing water than the Hoover Dam holds back — a full reservoir, in a coupe the size of a laundry basket, appearing from a sky that wasn't even raining that hard.

It is, in every way that matters and several that don't, a remarkable machine.

07One last record he never saw

Jim Mariol died in January 2020, at 89, in Cincinnati — the grandfather of industrial design in that city, remembered above everything for a toy. He'd spent his life around real cars; in his own driveway, at the end, sat a 1936 Packard Convertible Coupe, the car of a man who'd finally arrived. He never designed a real one. He designed the one that mattered.

Two months after he died, the world locked down. In March 2020, with parents across Britain suddenly facing weeks indoors with feral, energetic toddlers, they bought more than 85,000 Cozy Coupes in a single month — enough to once again outsell every gasoline-powered car in the country. Forty-one years after he scooted backward across his office floor and had the idea, Jim Mariol's little red coupe set one more record. He wasn't there to see it. It's the kind of ending he'd probably have found very funny.

The Verdict

No windows, no working horn, no steering to speak of, and a top speed you could out-crawl. It is also the best-selling car in America, the best-loved vehicle on Earth, and the single most reliable joy-delivery device ever molded. Buy your kid the cheap one. Just don't leave it in the yard — and mind your shins.
